topic: Comparison, integral, ratio, and alternating-series tests
subtitle: Comparison, integral, ratio, and alternating-series tests

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response states the limit comparison test --- a finite positive limit makes the two series behave alike --- names the comparison series as the convergent p-series with exponent two, and concludes that the given series converges. Full credit requires the positivity of the limit to be mentioned, since a limit of zero or infinity only gives a one-way conclusion.

Part (b): a correct response checks the three conditions the integral test needs --- the function is positive, continuous and decreasing on the interval --- before using the finite integral to conclude that the series converges. Full credit also says that the value of the integral is NOT the sum of the series.

problems.slot: the limit of the term sizes

problems.desc: Part (c): a correct response checks both conditions of the alternating series test --- the term sizes decrease and their limit is zero --- and then uses the remainder bound, which says the error after a partial sum is no larger than the first term left out. Full credit states the bound in that form rather than guessing a number of terms.

Part (b): a correct response names the comparison series as the p-series with exponent two, notes that the limit is finite and positive, and concludes convergence. Full credit explains the choice of comparison series --- keep the leading power on the top and the bottom, which leaves n over n cubed.

Part (b): a correct response reports that the ratio grows without bound, so the ratio test gives divergence. Full credit also observes that the terms themselves grow without bound, which is a second and independent reason --- factorial growth beats any fixed exponential.

Part (b): a correct response identifies the substitution u equal to the natural log of x, confirms the integrand is positive, continuous and decreasing beyond x equal to two, and concludes that the series converges because the improper integral is finite. Full credit names the substitution.

problems.slot: the error bound after five terms

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response shows the algebra that turns the ratio of consecutive terms into three times (n plus one) over n squared --- the factorial contributes one factor of n plus one in the denominator and the power of three contributes a single factor of three. Full credit shows that cancellation, since the whole difficulty of the ratio test lives there.

Part (c): a correct response argues that the ratio test is useless here because the limit of the ratio is one, and that limit comparison against the p-series with exponent two settles it instead. Full credit says WHY the ratio test fails on rational terms --- consecutive terms of a rational expression always have ratio approaching one --- rather than only reporting that it did.
